interview.a: The client initiates the data connection to the server's advertised passive port, avoiding a server-initiated inbound connection to the client's private address.

title: SMTP
summary: How mail moves between MTAs. Store-and-forward, MX records, and spam as an adversarial load.
what: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) transfers email between mail clients and mail transfer agents and between mail servers. It is a store-and-forward protocol: a server may accept a message for delivery and attempt onward transfer later.
why: Email crosses independently operated domains, so the system must route messages, queue temporary failures, authenticate senders where possible, and mitigate spam and abuse.
mental: An SMTP server accepts a message envelope and content, then relays it toward the recipient domain's mail server. Acceptance means responsibility for further delivery under the service contract, not proof the message reached the inbox.
points: DNS MX records identify mail exchangers for a recipient domain; fallback behavior and DNS rules matter when no MX exists.
SMTP uses commands and status replies such as EHLO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, and QUIT.
STARTTLS or implicit TLS protects a connection when correctly negotiated, while SMTP AUTH authenticates a submitting client.
SPF, DKIM, and DMARC address different aspects of domain authorization, message signing, and policy/reporting.
Mail servers queue messages and retry temporary failures; permanent failures generally produce a bounce or status report.
steps: A sender submits mail to an authenticated submission server.
The sender domain or sending MTA resolves the destination domain's mail exchanger.
The sending MTA opens SMTP, negotiates capabilities/TLS, and submits envelope plus message data.
The receiving MTA accepts or rejects the message, then local policy and filtering determine eventual mailbox delivery.
usage: Diagnosing failed delivery and SMTP authentication problems.
Understanding MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC, queues, and bounces.
mistakes: Assuming SMTP acceptance guarantees inbox placement.
Confusing the SMTP envelope sender with the From header shown to the user.
Assuming TLS alone proves that the visible From domain is authorized.

interview.q: What is the role of an MX record?
interview.a: It identifies mail servers responsible for receiving email for a domain, with preference values used to choose among records.

interview.q: What does DKIM provide?
interview.a: It provides a cryptographic signature over selected message content/headers so receivers can verify that the signed parts were not altered and that a signing domain took responsibility.

title: SSH
summary: Authenticated, encrypted remote shells and tunnels. Keys, not passwords, if you can.
what: Secure Shell (SSH) is a protocol suite for authenticated and encrypted remote command execution, file transfer, and tunneling. It commonly authenticates servers using host keys and clients using passwords, public keys, certificates, or other configured methods.
why: SSH provides a secure administrative channel across untrusted networks. Secure use depends on host identity verification, key hygiene, access control, patching, and minimizing exposed services.
mental: The client first establishes an encrypted channel and verifies the server's host identity, then authenticates the user. Encryption without correct host-key verification can protect traffic to an impostor.
points: SSH host keys let clients detect server identity changes; blindly accepting unknown keys weakens this protection.
Public-key authentication lets the client prove possession of a private key without sending that private key to the server.
SSH agent forwarding and port forwarding introduce trust and exposure considerations.
SCP, SFTP, and remote shell capabilities use SSH in different ways and have distinct semantics.
Least privilege, key rotation, restrictive authorized_keys options, and disabling unnecessary account access improve security.
steps: The client connects to the server and negotiates algorithms/keys.
It verifies the server host key according to the user's trust configuration.
The client authenticates the user with an allowed method.
The client opens a shell, command channel, file transfer, or tunnel according to server policy.
usage: Secure remote administration and deployment workflows.
SFTP file transfer and local/remote port forwarding.
mistakes: Disabling host-key checking as a routine workaround.
Sharing private keys or leaving them unprotected.
Assuming SSH tunnels automatically add application-layer authentication or authorization.

interview.q: What is the purpose of an SSH host key?
interview.a: It allows a client to identify the server endpoint and detect unexpected identity changes, helping prevent man-in-the-middle attacks.

interview.q: Why can agent forwarding be risky?
interview.a: A remote host may be able to request signatures through the forwarded agent while the session is active, so forwarding increases the trust placed in that host.

title: WebSockets
summary: A TCP-backed, full-duplex channel started with an HTTP upgrade.
what: WebSocket is a protocol for bidirectional messages over a single persistent connection. The classic browser flow begins with an HTTP upgrade handshake; WebSocket frames then carry messages until either endpoint closes the connection.
why: Polling repeatedly requests updates even when nothing changes. WebSockets let servers push messages to connected clients and let either side send data with lower request overhead, at the cost of persistent connection management.
mental: After the handshake, the connection is no longer a series of ordinary HTTP request-response exchanges. The application must define message types, authentication, backpressure, reconnect behavior, and lifecycle handling.
points: The initial handshake uses HTTP semantics, including Upgrade and appropriate response headers; browser security also considers origin and cookies.
Frames may be split into fragments; message framing is different from TCP's byte-stream boundaries.
The protocol defines ping/pong control frames and close-handshake behavior.
Authentication and authorization still belong to the application/session design; an open socket can outlive a token or permission change unless handled.
Persistent connections require limits, heartbeats/timeouts, bounded send queues, and cleanup during deploys or network changes.
steps: The client establishes HTTP(S) and requests a WebSocket upgrade.
The server validates the handshake, policy, and required authentication/origin information.
Both sides exchange application messages over the persistent connection.
On network loss or shutdown, the app handles reconnect/backoff and restores state safely.
usage: Live dashboards, chat, collaborative editing, and game state updates.
Replacing frequent polling when both sides benefit from server push.
mistakes: Assuming WebSocket messages align with individual TCP packets or reads.
Failing to revalidate authorization when a long-lived socket remains open.
Allowing unbounded outbound queues when clients consume messages slowly.

interview.q: How does WebSocket differ from ordinary HTTP polling?
interview.a: WebSocket keeps a persistent bidirectional channel after an upgrade handshake, avoiding repeated request setup for each update.

interview.q: What must an application add beyond the WebSocket protocol?
interview.a: Message schema, authorization, resource limits/backpressure, reconnect semantics, validation, and operational monitoring.

title: Constraints
summary: Declarations the engine enforces: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, FK — integrity that survives a bad insert.
what: Database constraints are rules enforced by the DBMS to keep stored data valid. Common examples include NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, and FOREIGN KEY constraints.
why: Applications have multiple writers—APIs, scripts, batch jobs, and administrators. Constraints protect data invariants at the storage boundary instead of trusting every caller to implement validation correctly.
mental: Put an invariant as close as possible to the data it protects. An application can still validate early for a better user experience, but the database constraint is the final enforcement layer.
points: NOT NULL forbids a missing value in a column, while CHECK restricts values or row-level relationships according to the database's semantics.
UNIQUE constrains duplicate key values, with NULL handling varying by database and constraint form.
PRIMARY KEY combines uniqueness and non-null identity for rows.
FOREIGN KEY enforces references to an eligible key in another relation.
Constraint timing and deferrability vary across database systems; check the engine's documentation for complex transactions.
steps: Write down the business invariant in precise terms.
Choose a constraint type that expresses it in the schema.
Add the constraint through a migration, handling existing invalid rows first.
Test valid and invalid inserts/updates from different access paths.
usage: Protecting unique emails, nonnegative quantities, valid references, and mandatory fields.
Keeping integrity consistent across API endpoints and scheduled jobs.
mistakes: Treating frontend validation as sufficient for integrity.
Writing a CHECK constraint without understanding NULL/three-valued logic.
Assuming a foreign key provides authorization or hides rows from unauthorized users.

interview.q: Why add database constraints if the API already validates input?
interview.a: Constraints protect invariants across every writer and prevent races or non-API writes from bypassing application checks.

interview.q: Is a foreign key an access-control mechanism?
interview.a: No. It validates referential integrity; permissions and row-level authorization require separate controls.

title: Aggregation
summary: GROUP BY, HAVING, and the reduction of many rows to a statistic.
what: SQL aggregation reduces multiple rows to summary values using functions such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, and MAX. GROUP BY forms groups based on selected expressions, and HAVING filters those groups after aggregate values are computed.
why: Aggregations answer reporting and analytical questions without requiring the application to fetch every row and compute totals itself. Correct grouping and join semantics are essential to avoid counting duplicated rows.
mental: WHERE filters input rows first; GROUP BY partitions the remaining rows; aggregate functions reduce each group; HAVING filters the groups; SELECT returns expressions allowed by the query's grouping rules.
points: COUNT(*) counts rows, while COUNT(column) excludes rows where that column is NULL.
WHERE filters individual rows before grouping; HAVING filters aggregate groups.
GROUP BY on several columns creates a group for each distinct combination under the DBMS's comparison rules.
Joins can multiply rows before aggregation, creating inflated sums/counts if the intended grain is not preserved.
Indexes, statistics, and hash/sort aggregation choices affect execution cost.
steps: Decide the result's grain, such as one row per customer or per month.
Join only the data needed and verify the join does not unintentionally multiply facts.
Filter individual rows with WHERE and form groups with GROUP BY.
Use aggregate expressions and HAVING to filter groups, then check counts against a small hand-calculated example.
usage: Calculating order totals, monthly active users, average scores, and inventory summaries.
Building dashboards and reports over relational data.
mistakes: Using WHERE to test an aggregate result when HAVING is required.
Confusing COUNT(*) with COUNT(nullable_column).
Summing a parent amount after joining to multiple child rows and double-counting it.

interview.q: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
interview.a: WHERE filters input rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups based on aggregate or grouped expressions.

interview.q: Why can a join inflate an aggregate?
interview.a: A one-to-many join can repeat a fact row once for each matching child, so aggregate sums/counts may no longer represent the intended grain.

title: Subqueries
summary: A query used as a value, a table, or a predicate. Correlated vs uncorrelated is the performance fork.
what: A subquery is a query nested inside another SQL statement. It can return a scalar value, a single-column set for IN/ANY/ALL, a row relation in FROM, or a Boolean condition through EXISTS.
why: Subqueries express dependencies between query results and can make existence tests, comparisons, and derived relations easier to read. Their performance depends on correlation, indexes, cardinality, and optimizer transformations.
mental: First identify how the inner query is used. An uncorrelated subquery can often be evaluated independently; a correlated one references outer rows, though optimizers may rewrite it as a join or another plan.
points: Scalar subqueries must meet the database's cardinality rules, often returning at most one row and one column.
EXISTS tests whether the inner query returns any row, and the projection value itself is usually irrelevant.
Correlated subqueries reference outer-query columns; logical correlation does not always imply literal repeated execution.
NOT IN can behave unexpectedly if the subquery returns NULL because SQL comparisons use three-valued logic; NOT EXISTS is often safer for anti-joins.
The optimizer may decorrelate or transform subqueries, so inspect the plan instead of assuming a fixed execution pattern.
steps: Write the inner query independently and verify its intended result shape.
Connect it to the outer query through a scalar comparison, IN, EXISTS, or FROM relation.
Check NULL, empty-set, and multiple-row behavior.
Use EXPLAIN to see how the DBMS executes the final query on representative data.
usage: Find customers who have at least one order using EXISTS.
Compare a row against an aggregate or retrieve a derived table for subsequent joins.
mistakes: Using NOT IN without accounting for NULLs in the inner result.
Assuming every correlated subquery executes once per outer row.
Writing a scalar subquery that unexpectedly returns multiple rows.

interview.q: When is EXISTS useful?
interview.a: When the query only needs to know whether at least one matching row exists, especially for semijoin/anti-join logic.

interview.q: Why can NOT IN return no rows unexpectedly?
interview.a: If the inner set contains NULL, comparisons can become UNKNOWN; WHERE keeps only TRUE. A carefully correlated NOT EXISTS often expresses the intended condition better.

title: Views
summary: Named queries. Virtual by default; materialized when you cache the result.
what: A view is a named query that presents a virtual relation to callers. An ordinary view stores the query definition rather than a separate copy of its results; a materialized view stores results and must be refreshed or maintained.
why: Views can simplify repeated query logic, provide a stable logical interface, and restrict which columns/rows a client sees. They do not automatically make an expensive query fast or enforce every form of security.
mental: A regular view behaves like a reusable query expression. A materialized view behaves more like a cached result, trading storage and freshness/refresh complexity for faster reads.
points: A regular view generally reflects current underlying data according to the transaction's visibility rules when queried.
A materialized view may be stale until refreshed or incrementally maintained.
Views can provide abstraction when underlying table structure changes, subject to compatibility and dependency constraints.
Security depends on the DBMS's view/definer/invoker and privilege semantics; a view alone is not universally a complete authorization boundary.
Complex views may be expanded into larger queries and optimized along with the caller's statement.
steps: Define a view around a useful projection/filter/join over underlying tables.
Grant the relevant caller access to the view and choose underlying privilege semantics carefully.
Inspect the query plan if the view is slow; its logic may expand into joins, filters, or sorts.
For materialized results, define refresh timing and acceptable staleness.
usage: Providing a stable schema for reports and application queries.
Exposing a limited column set for a specific consumer.
Caching expensive aggregates through materialized views.
mistakes: Assuming an ordinary view stores data or improves performance automatically.
Ignoring materialized-view staleness and refresh failures.
Treating the existence of a view as proof that sensitive underlying data are inaccessible.

interview.q: How does a materialized view differ from a regular view?
interview.a: A regular view stores a query definition and computes results when used; a materialized view stores query results and needs refresh/maintenance.

interview.q: Can views help with security?
interview.a: They can expose only selected data with appropriate privilege configuration, but the exact security boundary depends on database semantics and grants.

title: 2NF
summary: 1NF plus no partial dependence of a non-key attribute on part of a composite key.
what: Second Normal Form (2NF) requires a relation to be in 1NF and every non-prime attribute to depend on the whole of each candidate key, not merely a proper subset. Partial dependencies matter primarily when candidate keys are composite.
why: Partial dependencies repeat facts unnecessarily. Decomposing them reduces update anomalies and ensures each non-key fact is tied to the complete identity it describes.
mental: If the key is (student_id, course_id), ask whether an attribute needs both values to be determined. A student's name depends only on student_id, so it belongs with the student, not the enrollment pair.
points: 2NF is evaluated against candidate keys and functional dependencies, not just whether the table has a primary key.
A table with only single-attribute candidate keys has no partial dependency on a proper subset of such a key.
Non-prime attributes are attributes that are not part of any candidate key.
Decomposition should preserve information through a lossless join; dependency preservation should also be considered.
2NF does not remove every transitive dependency; 3NF addresses another class of dependency.
steps: Identify all candidate keys and functional dependencies.
Find any non-prime attribute determined by only a proper subset of a composite key.
Move those dependent attributes into a relation keyed by that subset.
Keep a relation for the original full-key fact and join relations back by their key.
usage: Normalizing enrollment, order-line, and other composite-key tables.
Solving normalization questions by listing dependencies.
mistakes: Checking 2NF using only the chosen primary key while ignoring other candidate keys.
Thinking a repeated value automatically proves a 2NF violation without examining functional dependencies.
Assuming 2NF automatically implies 3NF.

interview.q: What is a partial dependency?
interview.a: A non-prime attribute depends on a proper subset of a candidate key, rather than on the entire candidate key.

interview.q: When is a relation automatically in 2NF with respect to partial dependency?
interview.a: When every candidate key is a single attribute, there is no proper nonempty subset of that key on which a partial dependency could exist.

title: 3NF
summary: 2NF plus no transitive dependence of a non-key attribute on the key.
what: Third Normal Form (3NF) requires 2NF and constrains nontrivial functional dependencies so that the determinant is a superkey or the dependent attribute is prime, under the formal definition. Introductory lessons often describe this as removing transitive dependencies of non-key attributes on a key.
why: Transitive dependencies can repeat facts that belong to another entity. Separating those facts reduces anomalies while allowing the original view to be reconstructed using joins.
mental: A key should determine attributes that describe the row's entity. If key→department_id and department_id→department_name, storing department_name with each employee repeats a department fact that can change independently.
points: A functional dependency X→Y means rows with equal X values must have equal Y values.
3NF's formal definition must be checked across candidate keys, prime attributes, and all relevant functional dependencies.
A simple transitive dependency of a non-key attribute on the key is a common 3NF violation pattern.
A 3NF synthesis can preserve dependencies under the standard assumptions, while BCNF decomposition may not preserve all dependencies.
Normalization aims for lossless and maintainable design, not the maximum possible number of tables.
steps: List candidate keys and known functional dependencies.
Look for non-key facts determined by another non-key determinant.
Move that fact and determinant into a separate relation with a key, keeping a reference where needed.
Check that the decomposition is lossless and preserves required constraints.
usage: Removing duplicated department, supplier, or category descriptions from transactional tables.
Explaining why 3NF and BCNF differ.
mistakes: Defining 3NF only by table appearance rather than functional dependencies.
Assuming every determinant must be a superkey; that is the stricter BCNF rule.
Decomposing without checking if joins reconstruct the original facts.

interview.q: What does 3NF try to prevent?
interview.a: It rules out certain dependencies that make non-key facts depend transitively on a candidate key, subject to the formal 3NF definition.

interview.q: How is BCNF stricter than 3NF?
interview.a: BCNF requires every determinant of a nontrivial functional dependency to be a superkey, while 3NF allows a dependency when its right-hand side is prime.

title: BCNF
summary: Every determinant is a candidate key. Stricter than 3NF; sometimes you lose a dependency.
what: Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) requires that for every nontrivial functional dependency X→Y, X is a superkey. It is stricter than 3NF and focuses on whether every determinant can identify a row.
why: Some relations satisfy 3NF yet retain redundancy because a non-superkey determinant determines another attribute. BCNF removes that class of dependency anomaly, though a decomposition can lose dependency preservation.
mental: For each meaningful determinant, ask whether knowing it identifies an entire tuple. If not, the dependency may require decomposition under BCNF.
points: A superkey functionally determines all attributes of the relation; a candidate key is a minimal superkey.
BCNF is violated by any nontrivial dependency whose determinant is not a superkey.
BCNF decomposition is lossless under the standard decomposition step based on a violating dependency.
BCNF decomposition may fail to preserve every original dependency, so constraints can become harder to enforce without joins.
Formal analysis needs the set of functional dependencies, not just observed example rows.
steps: Determine candidate keys and relevant functional dependencies.
Find a nontrivial dependency X→Y where X is not a superkey.
Decompose the relation into projections that separate the violating dependency.
Verify the decomposition is lossless, then check which dependencies remain locally enforceable.
usage: Advanced database normalization problems.
Evaluating the trade-off between BCNF and dependency-preserving 3NF schemas.
mistakes: Assuming BCNF always preserves every functional dependency.
Confusing superkeys with minimal candidate keys.
Inferring functional dependencies only from a small set of sample tuples.

interview.q: What condition defines BCNF?
interview.a: For every nontrivial functional dependency X→Y, X must be a superkey.

interview.q: What is one trade-off of BCNF decomposition?
interview.a: It is lossless for the standard violating-dependency decomposition but may not preserve all dependencies locally, requiring joins or additional enforcement.

title: Storage Engines
summary: The physical implementation: heap files, clustered indexes, InnoDB vs MyISAM vs LSM.
what: A database storage engine implements the physical layout and persistence of records and indexes. Engines may use heap pages, B+ tree indexes, log-structured merge trees, write-ahead logs, buffer pools, and engine-specific concurrency/recovery rules.
why: The storage engine determines much of the database's write/read profile, durability, compression, indexing, and maintenance behavior. Logical SQL alone does not reveal these costs.
mental: Separate the logical database from physical storage. A query plan chooses operators; the storage engine decides how rows/pages/indexes are laid out and how changes survive failure.
points: Heap or heap-like tables store records in pages without requiring every row to be physically ordered by a key.
B+ tree indexes support point and range access with page-oriented balanced trees.
LSM-tree designs batch writes through memory structures and immutable sorted runs, trading compaction/write behavior against read amplification.
WAL or another recovery mechanism records sufficient information to restore a consistent state after crash.
Engine choice and settings affect locking/MVCC, compression, durability, and operational maintenance; compare actual product documentation.
steps: Choose a logical schema and query workload.
Inspect the engine's row/index layout and write path.
Measure query plans, cache behavior, and write amplification using representative data.
Plan backup, recovery, compaction/checkpoint/vacuum, and schema maintenance around the chosen engine.
usage: Choosing between row-oriented transactional storage and columnar analytical storage.
Explaining why storage engine and index design affect performance.
mistakes: Assuming every SQL database has identical physical storage and concurrency behavior.
Choosing an engine from generic benchmarks without matching the workload.
Treating a replicated copy as a replacement for backups and recovery tests.

interview.q: What is a storage engine?
interview.a: The database subsystem responsible for physical record/index organization, persistence, and associated storage-level operations.

interview.q: Why might an LSM tree suit write-heavy workloads?
interview.a: It can batch and sequentialize writes, although compaction and read amplification impose their own costs.

title: Partitioning
summary: Splitting a table by range, list, or hash — within one instance or across them.
what: Partitioning splits one logical table or index into smaller physical partitions according to a key or rule such as range, list, or hash. In many systems the partitions remain within one database instance, unlike sharding across independent nodes.
why: Partitioning can improve maintenance, data lifecycle operations, pruning for selective queries, and manageability of large tables. It does not guarantee faster queries and can complicate unique constraints and partition-key choice.
mental: A partitioning rule sends each row to a physical subset. If a query filters on the partition key, the database may skip irrelevant partitions; otherwise it may need to visit many or all of them.
points: Range partitioning groups values such as dates into intervals and can simplify dropping old data.
Hash partitioning distributes keys across partitions and can reduce skew when the hash distribution is suitable.
List partitioning maps values to named partitions, often for regions or categories.
Partition pruning works when the planner can relate query predicates to the partition bounds.
Partitioning and sharding are distinct: partitioned data may still belong to one DBMS instance and failure domain.
steps: Choose a partition key aligned with data lifecycle or query predicates.
Define bounds/list/hash rules and create representative test partitions.
Check whether important queries prune partitions in their execution plans.
Plan indexes, constraints, data movement, and maintenance for growing partitions.
usage: Partitioning large event tables by date.
Dropping expired data by partition rather than row-by-row deletion.
Reducing scan scope for frequently filtered queries.
mistakes: Partitioning by a key that creates an empty/overloaded hot partition.
Assuming every query will prune partitions automatically.
Confusing table partitioning with distribution across multiple independent servers.

interview.q: What is partition pruning?
interview.a: The optimizer excludes partitions that cannot contain rows matching the query predicates and partition bounds.

interview.q: How does partitioning differ from sharding?
interview.a: Partitioning often divides a table within one database instance; sharding distributes partitions or key ranges across separate nodes or instances.

title: Key-Value Stores
summary: The simplest NoSQL: get/put by key. Redis, Dynamo-style systems.
what: A key-value store associates each key with a value and offers operations such as GET, PUT, and DELETE. Values may be opaque bytes, serialized objects, or structured data depending on the product.
why: Key-value stores provide a simple access pattern for caching, sessions, counters, and lookup-heavy workloads. They can offer high throughput, but query capabilities and transaction guarantees depend on the implementation.
mental: A key is the lookup handle; the value is retrieved without necessarily searching fields inside it. If the access pattern needs arbitrary predicates or joins, a relational or document model may fit better.
points: Key distribution and partition strategy affect load balancing in distributed key-value systems.
TTL and eviction policies can be central for cache workloads; persistent stores have different durability goals.
Atomicity scope may be limited to one key or operation, or may be broader in particular databases.
Serialization format and schema versioning still matter even when the server treats values as opaque.
Cache misses, stale values, and invalidation are application-level correctness concerns.
steps: Choose a stable key that represents the lookup needed by the application.
Serialize the value with an explicit schema/version where needed.
Use GET/PUT/DELETE and define TTL, persistence, and consistency behavior.
Handle cache misses, errors, and invalidation without assuming the value always exists.
usage: Session stores, lookup tables, caches, and idempotency-key registries.
Storing small values that are retrieved by known key.
mistakes: Using ever-growing unbounded keys/values with no eviction or retention plan.
Treating cached values as authoritative when invalidation is not reliable.
Expecting relational joins or arbitrary filtering from a pure key-value access model.

interview.q: When is a key-value store a natural fit?
interview.a: When applications primarily retrieve or replace values by known key and do not need broad relational queries over value fields.

interview.q: What makes cache invalidation difficult?
interview.a: The application must keep cached copies aligned with changing source data across races, failures, TTLs, and multiple readers.

title: Document Stores
summary: JSON/BSON documents with secondary indexes. Schema-on-read, query-on-fields.
what: A document store persists records as structured documents, commonly JSON-like objects with nested fields and arrays. It typically supports key lookups and indexes or queries on selected document fields.
why: Document stores can fit variable-shaped entities and aggregate-like reads without decomposing every nested object into separate tables. Schema flexibility shifts some validation and migration discipline to application design.
mental: Treat each document as an aggregate boundary chosen around common reads and updates. Embed data that is naturally owned and used together; reference data that changes independently or must be shared widely.
points: Documents often have a unique identifier and may be indexed by selected fields or paths.
Embedding supports locality but can duplicate facts and enlarge writes when nested values change.
Referencing avoids some duplication but may require extra round trips or joins/lookups.
Schema flexibility does not mean no schema; applications still need validation and backward-compatible migrations.
Atomicity, transaction boundaries, indexing, and consistency differ across document databases.
steps: Model the data around the document's access patterns and update boundaries.
Choose which fields to embed and which to reference.
Define required fields, types, indexes, and versioning rules.
Test common queries and updates against realistic document sizes and cardinality.
usage: Product catalogs, content metadata, event payloads, and nested aggregate records.
Workloads where entities have variable fields and are usually read together.
mistakes: Embedding unbounded arrays that make documents too large or updates expensive.
Assuming flexible fields remove the need for validation and migrations.
Denormalizing shared facts without a plan to keep copies consistent.

interview.q: When would you embed instead of reference a document's related data?
interview.a: Embed when the data is bounded, owned by the parent, and usually read/updated together; reference when it is shared, unbounded, or independently managed.

interview.q: Does schema flexibility eliminate schema design?
interview.a: No. Applications still need validation, versioning, index design, and rules for fields that readers and writers expect.

title: Column Stores
summary: Values stored by column, not row. Analytics, compression, and vectorized execution.
what: A column-oriented database stores or processes values by column rather than row-oriented records. Analytical systems use columnar layout, compression, and vectorized execution to scan a few columns across many rows efficiently.
why: Analytical queries often aggregate a small subset of fields across millions or billions of rows. Columnar storage can reduce I/O and improve compression when the query does not need every field.
mental: A row store is efficient when an operation needs a complete record; a column store is efficient when it needs a few attributes from many records. Modern systems may use hybrid layouts or row groups rather than a pure choice.
points: Columnar layout avoids reading unrelated columns for projection-heavy analytical queries.
Similar values compress well, reducing I/O and storage when the data distribution is suitable.
Vectorized execution processes batches of values to reduce per-row overhead and improve CPU utilization.
Point updates and small transaction-oriented reads can be less natural in some columnar systems, depending on implementation.
Partitioning, sorting, clustering, and statistics remain important for scan pruning and query planning.
steps: Identify the analytical query's selected columns and filter predicates.
The engine prunes irrelevant partitions/row groups and reads only required column chunks.
It decompresses and processes vectors of values for filters and aggregates.
The query combines partial results and returns the required rows or summaries.
usage: Business intelligence, telemetry analytics, data warehouses, and large aggregations.
Scanning massive tables when most columns are irrelevant to the query.
mistakes: Assuming all column stores are unsuitable for updates; modern systems vary widely.
Choosing columnar storage solely because the table has many columns without studying the workload.
Ignoring sort order and pruning when optimizing scans.

interview.q: Why do column stores compress well?
interview.a: Values from the same column often have similar types and distributions, making encoding and compression more efficient than mixed row payloads.

interview.q: Why are column stores common in analytics?
interview.a: Analytical queries often scan a subset of columns across many rows, so columnar layout reduces I/O and supports vectorized processing.

title: Graph Databases
summary: First-class nodes and edges. Index-free adjacency and graph query languages.
what: A graph database represents entities as nodes and their relationships as edges, often with properties on both. It is designed for traversals and queries where relationship structure is central rather than incidental.
why: Relational joins can become complex for variable-depth relationships, such as social connections, network dependencies, or fraud rings. Graph storage/query models make traversals more natural, but do not automatically outperform relational databases for every workload.
mental: The main question is often who is connected to whom and how. Start from a node, follow edge types and direction, and constrain traversal depth and predicates.
points: Nodes represent entities; edges represent directed or undirected relationships according to the model.
Properties can annotate nodes and edges, while labels/types constrain traversal and indexing.
Index-free adjacency is an implementation concept in some graph systems, not a universal performance guarantee for all graph databases.
Traversal cost depends on degree distribution, path depth, filtering, and data placement.
Some workloads are better expressed as SQL joins or recursive queries; choose by access pattern and operational requirements.
steps: Identify the entities and relationships the application must query.
Choose node/edge types, direction, properties, and uniqueness constraints.
Create indexes for the entry points used by queries.
Bound traversals and inspect performance on highly connected nodes as well as typical data.
usage: Recommendation graphs, dependency maps, identity relationships, and path analysis.
Queries involving multi-hop relationships or variable-depth paths.
mistakes: Assuming a graph database is automatically faster for every connected-data problem.
Allowing unbounded traversals over hubs with huge degree.
Failing to model edge direction and relationship semantics carefully.

interview.q: When might a graph database be a good choice?
interview.a: When central queries traverse variable-depth or dense relationships and the graph model expresses those operations naturally.

interview.q: What can make graph traversals expensive?
interview.a: Large branching factors, deep paths, poor entry-point selectivity, and distributed data movement can cause huge traversal work.

title: Wi-Fi
summary: 802.11: association, airtime, and a MAC that is nothing like a switched Ethernet.
what: Wi-Fi is a family of IEEE 802.11 wireless LAN standards. Stations associate with an access point or operate in supported peer modes, share radio channels, and use link-layer procedures to coordinate transmission and protect frames.
why: Wi-Fi provides mobility without cabling but shares airtime and depends on radio conditions, authentication, roaming, and channel planning. Its performance differs from switched full-duplex Ethernet even when both ultimately carry IP packets.
mental: Stations listen and contend for a shared radio medium; acknowledgements and retransmissions help deal with collisions or errors. Throughput is a property of the whole airtime ecosystem, not just an advertised PHY rate.
points: CSMA/CA and link-layer acknowledgements help coordinate use of a shared medium; it is not the same as classic Ethernet CSMA/CD.
Association connects the station to the WLAN; WPA2/WPA3 security settings determine authentication and encryption behavior.
Rate adaptation responds to radio quality and retry performance.
Roaming across APs depends on client decisions, network configuration, and supported 802.11 features.
Channel interference, adjacent/co-channel networks, walls, and airtime contention can dominate speed.
steps: A station discovers the SSID and chooses an AP.
It associates and completes the security handshake.
It exchanges data using the selected PHY mode and channel-access behavior.
If signal quality or AP association changes, it adapts rate or roams while higher-level sessions may continue or recover.
usage: Deploying home, campus, and enterprise wireless LANs.
Troubleshooting retransmissions, roaming, and crowded channels.
mistakes: Assuming advertised Wi-Fi PHY rate equals application throughput.
Confusing authentication to the WLAN with authorization to every internal service.
Changing channels or power without measuring nearby co-channel interference.

interview.q: Why does Wi-Fi use collision avoidance rather than wired Ethernet's old collision detection?
interview.a: A wireless transmitter generally cannot reliably detect a collision while transmitting; 802.11 coordinates medium access and uses acknowledgements/retries.

interview.q: Why does client roaming vary across devices?
interview.a: Clients make roaming decisions using signal, scan behavior, supported features, and vendor algorithms, while AP configuration also influences the process.

title: BGP
summary: The internet's inter-domain routing protocol: path vectors, policy, and the default-free zone.
what: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) is a path-vector routing protocol used to exchange IP reachability between autonomous systems and in other policy-driven routing contexts. It selects routes using attributes and local policy rather than simply choosing the physically shortest path.
why: The global internet consists of independently operated networks with business and security policies. BGP allows operators to control which routes they announce and prefer, but configuration mistakes can leak or withdraw large numbers of routes.
mental: BGP advertisements include a destination prefix and path/policy attributes. A router applies import policy, selects a best path among eligible candidates, and applies export policy before advertising reachability onward.
points: AS_PATH records autonomous systems traversed and is used for loop prevention and policy decisions.
LOCAL_PREF influences preferred exit paths within an AS in common BGP policy; exact selection order follows the BGP implementation/policy.
NEXT_HOP must resolve for a route to be usable.
BGP can establish external (eBGP) or internal (iBGP) sessions; their rules and topology requirements differ.
Route filters, prefix limits, RPKI-based validation, and monitoring help reduce route-leak and hijack risks.
steps: Routers establish a BGP session with a peer and exchange capabilities and routes.
Import policy filters or modifies candidate advertisements.
The router selects eligible best paths using attributes and configured policy.
Export policy determines which routes to advertise to other peers; operators monitor changes and reachability.
usage: Interconnecting internet service providers and large enterprise networks.
Managing multiple upstream providers and controlled traffic engineering.
mistakes: Assuming BGP picks the lowest-latency or fewest-hop route by default.
Accepting all routes from a peer without appropriate filters and limits.
Confusing route announcement with proof of legitimate ownership or reachability at the destination.

interview.q: Why is BGP called policy-driven?
interview.a: Its path attributes and operator policies determine which routes are accepted, preferred, and exported; the selected route is not simply the shortest physical path.

interview.q: How does AS_PATH help?
interview.a: It lists ASes traversed and helps detect routing loops; operators also use it in route selection and policy.

title: OSPF
summary: A link-state IGP: flood LSAs, run Dijkstra, install routes in the RIB.
what: Open Shortest Path First (OSPF) is a link-state interior gateway protocol. Routers exchange link-state advertisements within areas, build a topology database, and run a shortest-path calculation to choose routes based on configured costs.
why: OSPF adapts to internal topology changes without manually configuring every route. Its areas and summarization support scale, but adjacency, area, metric, and network-type mismatches can prevent neighbors from exchanging usable routes.
mental: Every router learns a common view of the area's topology, then computes its own shortest paths from that view. The resulting routing table is local even though the topology database is shared.
points: OSPF uses neighbor relationships and link-state advertisements to distribute topology information.
Routers run Dijkstra's shortest-path-first algorithm against the link-state database.
Areas limit flooding scope and support hierarchical routing; Area 0 is the backbone in conventional multi-area designs.
Interface costs influence path preference; equal-cost multipath may install several next hops where supported.
Authentication, timers, MTU/network type, router IDs, and area settings must be compatible for adjacency.
steps: Interfaces send Hellos and discover eligible OSPF neighbors.
Neighbors establish adjacencies and synchronize relevant link-state databases.
Link-state changes are flooded and the router recomputes shortest paths.
The router installs routes and forwards packets using its forwarding plane.
usage: Routing inside enterprises, campuses, and provider networks.
Diagnosing a route absent because an OSPF adjacency or area design is wrong.
mistakes: Assuming OSPF is used between autonomous systems on the public internet; BGP typically serves that role.
Confusing an OSPF database entry with an installed forwarding route.
Changing costs without checking equal-cost paths and convergence impact.

interview.q: What algorithm does OSPF use for route calculation?
interview.a: It uses a shortest-path-first calculation based on the link-state topology and configured link costs.

interview.q: Why use OSPF areas?
interview.a: Areas constrain flooding and support hierarchical scale and summarization, while requiring an area design with a backbone connection in conventional multi-area OSPF.

title: Spanning Tree
summary: A loop-free active topology on a switched LAN. Without it, broadcasts amplify until the LAN dies.
what: Spanning Tree Protocol (STP) builds a loop-free active topology for redundant layer-2 Ethernet links. Switches exchange bridge protocol data units, elect a root bridge, and select port roles/states that block some forwarding paths while retaining backups.
why: Redundant L2 links improve resilience, but an unmanaged Ethernet loop can multiply broadcasts and destabilize MAC learning. STP keeps redundancy without allowing all physical links to forward at once.
mental: Treat the switches and links as a graph. STP selects one logical spanning tree from the redundant graph, then recalculates after topology changes so loops are avoided.
points: The root bridge is elected using bridge ID, based on priority and MAC-address tie-breaking.
Path costs help determine root ports and designated ports.
Blocked/non-forwarding ports provide alternate links that can be activated after a failure.
Rapid STP and vendor variants improve convergence, but exact timer and edge-port behavior matter.
PortFast/edge settings should only be applied to appropriate endpoint-facing ports; BPDU protections help prevent accidental switch loops.
steps: Switches exchange BPDUs and elect the root bridge.
Each non-root switch selects a root port for its best path to the root.
Each segment selects a designated port; redundant ports are placed in non-forwarding states.
When a link changes, the protocol recalculates and activates a safe alternate path.
usage: Designing redundant campus and enterprise switching.
Diagnosing broadcast storms and unexpected blocked ports.
mistakes: Connecting redundant switches without a loop-control design.
Enabling edge/PortFast behavior on a switch-to-switch connection without safeguards.
Assuming a blocked port is broken rather than intentionally preventing a loop.

interview.q: Why does STP block some healthy physical links?
interview.a: It removes redundant paths from the active layer-2 forwarding topology so frames cannot circulate indefinitely, while keeping backup links available.

interview.q: What determines the root bridge?
interview.a: The switch with the best bridge ID wins, normally based on configured priority and then MAC-address tie-breakers.

title: fork()
summary: Copy a process: the child gets 0, the parent gets a pid. Copy-on-write makes the copy cheap until a write.
what: On POSIX systems, fork() creates a child process from the calling process. The child starts with a logical copy of the parent's address space and inherited process attributes, while the return value distinguishes the child from the parent.
why: fork plus exec is a classic way to launch programs while preserving the parent process. Copy-on-write keeps initial memory duplication relatively cheap, but the child must still handle inherited descriptors and multithreaded-process rules correctly.
mental: After fork, parent and child continue from the same point but have separate process identities and logically separate memory. They may run in either order, so communication should use explicit IPC rather than assuming execution order.
points: In the parent, fork returns the child PID; in the child it returns zero; failure returns -1 in the parent and creates no child.
Copy-on-write initially shares physical pages where safe and copies pages when a process writes.
Open file descriptors are inherited and refer to the same underlying open file descriptions, affecting offsets and flags.
After fork in a multithreaded process, only the calling thread exists in the child; only async-signal-safe operations are safe until exec under POSIX rules.
Zombie children remain until their exit status is collected, typically via wait/waitpid or an equivalent mechanism.
steps: The parent calls fork and checks its return value.
The kernel creates the child task/process and sets up resource and memory semantics.
Parent and child continue independently; either may run first.
The child often calls exec to replace its program image, while the parent supervises or waits for its completion.
usage: Launching subprocesses in shells and service supervisors.
Understanding process trees, inherited file descriptors, and zombie cleanup.
mistakes: Assuming parent always executes before child.
Assuming fork eagerly copies all physical memory pages.
Calling unsafe library operations in a forked child of a multithreaded process before exec.

interview.q: What does fork return in parent and child?
interview.a: The parent receives the child's PID, the child receives 0, and the parent receives -1 on failure.

interview.q: Why must a multithreaded child be careful before exec?
interview.a: Only the calling thread survives in the child while locks may have been held by vanished threads; POSIX restricts pre-exec operations to async-signal-safe functions.

title: Working Set
summary: The pages a process is actually using. If they do not fit in RAM, the system thrashes.
what: A process's working set is the set of pages it has referenced during a chosen recent time window. It approximates the memory needed to keep that process's current locality resident and avoid frequent page faults.
why: Working-set information helps explain and prevent thrashing. Allocating fewer frames than an active working set may cause repeated eviction and reload of pages, wasting I/O and reducing useful CPU work.
mental: The working set moves as the application changes phases. A database scan, a graph traversal, and a compiler phase may need different page sets; the OS cannot assume one fixed number is best forever.
points: Working-set size depends on the measurement window and the program's current phase.
If the sum of active working sets exceeds available memory, some workloads may thrash.
Working-set models help reason about frame allocation and degree of multiprogramming.
Working-set estimates are approximations; pages referenced recently may not always be needed again soon.
Reducing memory footprint, limiting concurrency, or changing access locality can reduce pressure more effectively than adding CPU.
steps: Choose a recent reference window and track which pages were touched.
Estimate the current working-set size for each active process.
Compare the combined demand with available physical frames.
If demand exceeds capacity, reduce active memory pressure or adjust allocation and workload behavior.
usage: Diagnosing thrashing, high page faults, and low throughput under memory pressure.
Understanding locality in compilers, databases, and streaming data processing.
mistakes: Treating a working set as every page ever allocated by the process.
Assuming the estimate is independent of the chosen time window.
Responding to memory thrashing by increasing process concurrency without measurement.

interview.q: How does a working set relate to thrashing?
interview.a: When active working sets do not fit in physical memory, processes may repeatedly fault on pages that were recently evicted, causing excessive paging.

interview.q: Can a working set remain constant throughout a program?
interview.a: No. The set can change as the program moves between phases with different code, data, and access patterns.
